passage:
Monday: Jagdish kept glancing at the clock in class. His mother had stayed in bed that morning with a fever, and the fractions on the board swam past him. Preeti, his desk-mate, asked what was wrong, and he only shrugged.
Wednesday: He asked his father, "What can I do for Amma?" His father said he could fill her water jug after school and sit with her while she rested. That evening Jagdish also told his teacher, who nodded and said to come to her whenever it felt heavy.
Next Monday: Amma was up making tea. Jagdish still looked at the clock sometimes, but he finished his sums, and Preeti lent him her sharpener.

qa.q: Who sat next to Jagdish in class?
qa.a: Preeti, his desk-mate, sat next to him.

qa.q: Why did Jagdish keep glancing at the clock on Monday?
qa.a: He was worried about his mother, who had stayed in bed with a fever, and probably wanted to know how long until he could go home to her.

qa.q: What helped Jagdish more than worrying alone?
qa.a: Asking his father how he could help gave him small jobs to do, and telling his teacher meant he had another adult who knew. He did not have to make his mother well himself. 🙂

qa.q: How might Preeti have felt when Jagdish shrugged?
qa.a: Preeti may have felt unsure and a little concerned. She noticed something was wrong but did not push, and later she kindly lent him her sharpener.

grounding: A child worries about his unwell mother at school, asks how to help, keeps his routine and tells his teacher.

passage:
"Why does Chintu get the mango kulfi and I get nothing?" Kamal muttered.
"Because his throat is sore and the doctor said cold things soothe it," said his mother, Rukmini, sitting down next to him.
"You have been quiet all week."
"Everybody asks about Chintu. Nobody asks about me." Then, quickly, "I feel bad saying that."
"You can feel both, Kamal."
"Can we go for a walk, just us, on Saturday?"
"Yes. And you can help me carry his soup tray, if you like."
Kamal nodded. "I do want him better."

qa.q: What did Kamal say he felt bad saying?
qa.a: He said everyone asks about Chintu and nobody asks about him.

qa.q: What might Kamal be feeling when he says, "I do want him better"?
qa.a: He still cares about his brother even though he felt jealous; the sentence shows love and guilt mixed with his earlier resentment.

qa.q: What small step did Kamal ask for that could help him?
qa.a: He asked for a walk with his mother on Saturday, a bit of one-on-one time, which lets him keep caring for his brother without losing his own place.

qa.q: How might Rukmini see Kamal's complaint?
qa.a: Kamal's mother probably sees it as a normal reaction of a child who feels overlooked, and not as selfishness. She answers calmly and offers time and a task.

grounding: A child jealous of his sick brother's attention says so, feels guilty, and asks his mother for time; both feelings are accepted.

passage: The bus to the district hospital only ran twice a day, so Dhruv's father went alone most mornings. Dhruv's little sister Bindu was in a bed there with a bad chest. At home under the tamarind tree, Dhruv spread out his chalk stubs and drew a cow with a crooked smile, a kite and a tiny house with a yellow door for her. His friend Manoj called from the lane, "Come, we are playing kabaddi!" Dhruv hesitated, then ran off and laughed so hard he forgot the hospital for a while. When he came home he tucked the drawings into his father's bag and did not feel bad about the game.

qa.q: How many times a day did the bus to the district hospital run?
qa.a: It only ran twice a day.

qa.q: What might Dhruv have felt when he hesitated before joining the kabaddi game?
qa.a: He was probably torn between sadness for Bindu and the wish to play, perhaps wondering if it was wrong to have fun.

qa.q: What did Dhruv do that helped him stay connected to his sister while she was away?
qa.a: He drew pictures for her, like the cow, the kite and the house, and sent them with his father, so she would know he was thinking of her.

qa.q: How might Bindu feel when she sees the drawings in the hospital?
qa.a: Bindu may feel cheered and less lonely, knowing her brother was thinking of her. 😊

grounding: A child draws pictures for his younger sister in hospital and also plays; he may be sad and happy without guilt.

passage:
Friday: Yogesh had been counting days since the letter came. The cousins from Pune were coming Saturday. He cleaned the shelf and set out his carrom board and the building-block set.
Saturday: The cousins tumbled in with bags. Dhruv, the youngest, went straight for the blocks. Yogesh bit his lip, then said, "Take the red ones. I will show you how the bridge goes." Everyone got a turn at carrom, even the little ones.
Sunday: Yogesh caught himself saying, "No, you have to stand here!" Dhruv's face fell. Yogesh stopped, said, "Sorry, you pick the next game," and Dhruv grinned.

qa.q: Where were the cousins coming from?
qa.a: The cousins were coming from Pune.

qa.q: What was Yogesh feeling on Friday, and how can you tell?
qa.a: He was excited; he had been counting days since the letter came and cleaned the shelf to get ready.

qa.q: What went wrong on Sunday and how did Yogesh fix it?
qa.a: He started ordering Dhruv around and Dhruv's face fell. Yogesh stopped, said sorry and let Dhruv pick the next game.

qa.q: How might Dhruv have felt when Yogesh told Dhruv where to stand?
qa.a: Dhruv probably felt bossed around and a little hurt, since the fun turned into being told what to do until Yogesh apologised.

grounding: A child excited about visiting cousins shares toys and includes everyone, and corrects himself when he starts ordering people around.

passage: The hall was crowded and loud with wedding music, and Hrithik's uncle had to shout to be heard. "Pankaj got ninety-two in maths. What did you get, Hrithik?" Hrithik said his number quietly, and a relative shook her head and said, "Learn from your cousin." He looked at his sandals. Across the room Pankaj was standing beside the sweets, pushing his plate around, not eating. Later, on the terrace where it was quieter, Hrithik told his mother he felt small, and she squeezed his shoulder and said marks were not all of him. He thought, I am more than a number, and went to find Pankaj.

qa.q: What did Pankaj get in maths?
qa.a: He got ninety-two in maths.

qa.q: How was Hrithik feeling when he looked at his sandals?
qa.a: He felt small and hurt by being compared to his cousin.

qa.q: What did Hrithik do that helped him after the comparison?
qa.a: He told his mother how he felt, and she reassured him. Talking to a parent, rather than hiding the hurt, helped him remember he is more than his marks.

qa.q: How might Pankaj have felt at the sweets table?
qa.a: Pankaj may have felt judged and uncomfortable too, since he stood pushing his plate around and did not eat.

grounding: A child feels small when relatives compare his marks with his cousin's, tells his parent, and sees that the cousin may feel judged as well.

passage: Lalremsiami had been waiting for weeks to beat her cousin Shalini at cricket in the colony lane. Shalini's marks in maths were higher, and Lalremsiami wanted that to change. In the game she bowled her best over, and Shalini hit a boundary anyway. Lalremsiami felt a hot flash and thought, I want her to miss. She stopped, took a breath and noticed that this was too much. Then she asked, "How do you keep your wrist so still?" Shalini showed her. The next ball, Lalremsiami got her out. They both laughed. At homework time she asked Shalini to explain the maths trick too.

qa.q: Whose marks in maths were higher?
qa.a: Shalini's marks in maths were higher.

qa.q: What was Lalremsiami feeling when she thought, "I want her to miss"?
qa.a: She felt a hot rush of rivalry and jealousy, wanting her cousin to fail, and then realised it was more than friendly competition.

qa.q: What did Lalremsiami do next that turned the rivalry into something useful?
qa.a: She asked Shalini how she keeps her wrist still and later asked her to explain the maths trick, so she learned from her cousin's strengths.

qa.q: How might Shalini have seen Lalremsiami's question about her wrist?
qa.a: Shalini probably felt respected and pleased to be asked, which made the game friendlier for her too.

grounding: A child wants to beat her cousin at cricket and studies, notices when rivalry becomes wanting her to lose, and chooses to enjoy and learn from her.

passage: At the community centre's holiday camp, the art room was buzzing. Bidisha's two older cousins, Lakshmi and Rohan, had set up a board game at the big table and were laughing over private jokes. Bidisha stood by the door holding her paintbrush. Her throat felt tight. She walked over and asked, "Can I play too?" Rohan said the game was for two. She said, "Maybe we can start a new round with three?" Lakshmi shrugged, but Rohan still said no. Bidisha did not argue. She joined her friend Meena at the clay table and later told the camp helper what had happened, in a calm voice.

qa.q: What were Lakshmi and Rohan doing at the big table?
qa.a: They had set up a board game and were laughing over private jokes.

qa.q: What might Bidisha have been feeling when she stood by the door holding her paintbrush?
qa.a: She probably felt left out and hurt, and her tight throat shows the sting of being excluded.

qa.q: What could Bidisha try if the cousins keep leaving her out tomorrow?
qa.a: She could suggest a different game, keep playing with Meena, and, if it keeps happening, tell the camp helper or a family elder calmly, as she did.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi have seen the moment?
qa.a: Lakshmi may have gone along with Rohan without thinking much about Bidisha; the shrug suggests Lakshmi was unsure or did not want to disagree with Rohan.

grounding: A child is left out by two older cousins, asks to join, finds another friend, and calmly tells an adult.

passage: Saturday. Today Akash's face was red when I found him near the gate. Three boys from the next lane were laughing at his stammer and calling him names. My hands went cold. I wanted to shout, but I walked over, stood beside him and said, "That is my cousin. Please stop." My voice shook, but it came out calm. One boy smirked and they walked off, still muttering. Akash held my sleeve all the way home and whispered, "Thank you, didi." I told Chachi what happened, just in case they come back. I did not need to hit anyone, and I am glad. Aparna.

qa.q: Where did Aparna find Akash?
qa.a: She found Akash near the gate.

qa.q: What was Aparna feeling as she walked over to the boys?
qa.a: She was scared and angry: her hands went cold and she wanted to shout, but she stayed calm.

qa.q: Why did telling Chachi help, even though the boys had left?
qa.a: Telling an adult means someone else knows and can step in if the teasing returns, so Aparna and Akash are not alone with it.

qa.q: How might Akash have felt when Aparna stood beside him?
qa.a: Akash probably felt protected and relieved, which is shown by how he held her sleeve all the way home. 🤍

grounding: A child steps in calmly beside her small cousin who is being teased, then tells an adult; fighting was not needed.

passage: I sit two benches behind Harshita at lunch, so I saw it. She carried her tiffin to the table by the window where a group of girls from our class sat, and one of them said, "There is no space here," though there were two empty seats. She stood there a moment, then went and sat on the steps outside. I could not tell how she felt; her face was very still. The next day I told her I liked her drawing of the train, and she sat with me. She joined the art club after that. Later, I saw her talking to the class teacher quietly, so maybe she mentioned it. I am Tejas, from Class 6.

qa.q: Where did Harshita sit after she was turned away from the table?
qa.a: She sat on the steps outside.

qa.q: What might Harshita have been feeling on the steps, and why can Tejas not be sure?
qa.a: She may have felt hurt, but her face was very still, so Tejas cannot tell for certain whether it was hurt or just holding it in.

qa.q: What small step did Tejas take that helped?
qa.a: Tejas complimented Harshita's drawing of the train and made room for her, giving her one kind classmate to be near. Joining a club also gave her a place.

qa.q: What is it like for Tejas to watch this from two benches behind?
qa.a: Tejas sees the empty seats and the refusal clearly but cannot read Harshita's still face, so Tejas is left unsure, and that uncertainty turns into a kind word the next day.

grounding: A classmate observes a child being told by a group of girls that there is no place at their table; she finds one kind classmate, joins a club and speaks to a teacher.

passage: Rain drummed on the roof, so recess was indoors, and the whole class was squeezed between desks. Nazia watched Kavya's group giggle over sticker books in the corner. She wanted to sit with them so badly that her stomach ached. Then Kavya said, "You can sit here if you laugh at Bidisha's accent." Nazia's mouth went dry. Bidisha, her friend, was two rows away, drawing quietly. Nazia said, "No, thanks," and walked back. Bidisha looked up and moved her bag off the seat next to her. "I saved you one," she said. Nazia sat down. The sticker giggles kept going, but she found she could breathe.

qa.q: Why was recess indoors?
qa.a: It was raining, so recess was indoors.

qa.q: What was Nazia feeling as she watched Kavya's group?
qa.a: She envied them and wanted to belong, so much that her stomach ached.

qa.q: What could Nazia do if the popular group asks her again later?
qa.a: She can keep saying no to being unkind, stay with friends who accept her, and tell a teacher if the pressure continues.

qa.q: How might Bidisha have felt when Nazia walked back to her?
qa.a: Bidisha probably felt glad and touched that Nazia chose her, as her saved seat shows.

grounding: A child envies the popular group and is asked to mock a friend; she says no and finds real friendship.
